process_note: First reported on #34 as probably my own CPU contention: the file runs last in FILE_ORDER and I had run a 55-second board-free pytest in that window. The clean idle re-run reproduced it, so the self-blame was refuted. A plausible self-blame is still a hypothesis and still needs its control run - and it is more tempting than the other kind because accepting it costs nothing.
arms_note: All three arms are immutable commits. The third was 'current main' until mac-bench pointed out it was the one arm a later fix could make meaningless, so it was re-run pinned at f3cad64.

fix.licenses: the regression is gone at the rate this reproducer can see
fix.does_not_license: 'fixed'. 0 of 20 bounds the rate under 15%, not at zero, and #44's own 11-of-32 sits well inside that. Doubled from ten deliberately: at n=10 the rule of three reaches only 30%, a weaker claim than a bare '0 of 10' reads as.
fix.why_the_shape_is_right: Opening the gate when the drain ends rather than when start() does satisfies both invariants without depending on what start() happens to do afterwards. The earlier sketch rested on 'start() does no native reads after cmd()', true today and breakable silently by a future settle-read.

open: the Linux arm, linux-x1's, and the informative branch

mac-bench reports macOS does not reproduce the original regression either (0124e2b), so windows-desk is currently the only bench where the bug was visible - a fix validated only where it appeared leaves the other benches confirming nothing

levers.question: linux-x1's positive control showed CPU contention alone breaks this assertion on Linux. This asks whether contention and the commit are two routes on Windows as they are there.

contention.load: 56 busy loops on 28 cores (2x oversubscription, same ratio as linux-x1)
contention.verdict: contention is NOT a lever on this bench, at either commit

context.verdict: suite context IS the lever here, and multiplies the rate fourfold. The commit route exists in isolation - 3 of 20 is not zero - and context amplifies it.

cross_bench.linux-x1: CPU contention fires (5/6 loaded vs 0/5 idle, p=0.015)
cross_bench.windows-desk: suite context fires (6/10 vs 3/20, p=0.030); contention does not
cross_bench.means: One assertion, two platforms, two different levers, and each bench's lever is invisible to the other. linux-x1's idle unloaded runs could not have seen the context effect; windows-desk's idle contextual runs could not have seen the contention effect. That is why their 0 of 10 and this bench's 6 of 10 at the same commit were both correct.

not_claimed: that the contention failure and the commit failure are the same defect - they are the same ASSERTION failing, and pooling them would repeat #44's error of a headline incidence made of arms never run at one condition
that the fix is incomplete: at 37ce117 neither route reproduces here
levers.method_note: The reproducer held context fixed by accident - it was built by bisecting FILE_ORDER, not because context was known to be the lever. linux-x1's rule generalises: hold the machine's load fixed AND the test context fixed, or the measurement reports whichever the machine supplied.
